topics.title: What development promises: different people, different goals

concepts.label: Different People, Different Developmental Goals
concepts.cardText: Different persons seek different things: what is most important for them, given their aspirations. Landless rural labourers want more days of work and better wages; prosperous farmers from Punjab want higher support prices for their crops. Goals can even conflict: industrialists may want more dams for electricity, but dams may submerge land and displace people such as tribals. So different persons can have different developmental goals, and what is development for one may not be development for another; it may even be destructive.
concepts.hint: Would a landless labourer and a rich farmer want the same thing? Can one person's development hurt another?
concepts.probe: Why do different persons have different notions of development, and how can their goals conflict?
concepts.causeChain: Different life situations -> different aspirations and developmental goals -> goals may conflict (dams for industrialists displace tribals) -> what is development for one may be destructive for another

causeLinks.criterion: Connects people's different life situations and goals to the possibility that development for one group may not be development, or may even be destructive, for another.

keyPoints.text: Each one of them seeks different things. They seek things that are most important for them, i.e., that which can fulfil their aspirations or desires. For example, landless rural labourers want more days of work and better wages, while prosperous farmers from Punjab want a high family income through higher support prices for their crops.
keyPoints.followUp: Why do different people, like a landless labourer and a rich farmer, want different things from development?

checks.criterion: States that different persons seek different things, depending on what can fulfil their own aspirations (for example landless labourers versus prosperous farmers).

keyPoints.text: At times, two persons or groups may seek things which are conflicting. To get more electricity, industrialists may want more dams. But this may submerge the land and disrupt the lives of people who are displaced, such as tribals, who may prefer small check dams or tanks. So, different persons can have different developmental goals and what may be development for one may not be development for the other. It may even be destructive for the other.

concepts.label: Income and Other Goals
concepts.cardText: Most people want more income: regular work, better wages and decent prices for their crops. But people also seek equal treatment, freedom, security and respect of others, and resent discrimination. In some cases these matter more than income, because material goods are not all that you need to live. The quality of our life also depends on non-material things, and it is wrong to conclude that what cannot be measured is not important. So developmental goals are about better income and other important things in life.
concepts.hint: Would you take a job with high pay but no security and no time for your family?
concepts.probe: Besides income, what other goals do people seek, and why do they matter?
concepts.causeChain: People want more income, but also equal treatment, freedom, security and respect -> quality of life depends on non-material things too -> developmental goals are a mix of income and other goals

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the importance of non-material things like security, freedom and respect to people's developmental goals being a mix of income and other goals.

keyPoints.text: What people desire are regular work, better wages, and decent price for their crops or other products that they produce. In other words, they want more income.

checks.criterion: States that a common goal of people is more income (regular work, better wages, decent prices).

keyPoints.text: Besides seeking more income, people also seek things like equal treatment, freedom, security, and respect of others. They resent discrimination. In some cases, these may be more important than more income or more consumption because material goods are not all that you need to live. The quality of our life also depends on non-material things. It will be wrong to conclude that what cannot be measured is not important.

If women are engaged in paid work, their dignity in the household and society increases, and a safe and secure environment may allow more women to take up a variety of jobs. Hence, the developmental goals that people have are not only about better income but also about other important things in life.

checks.criterion: Concludes that people look at a mix of goals: development is not only about better income but also about other important things in life.

concepts.label: National Development
concepts.cardText: If individuals seek different goals, their notions of national development will also differ, and may even conflict. National development means thinking about questions such as: can all ideas be considered equally important; if there are conflicts, how does one decide; what would be a fair and just path for all; is there a better way of doing things; and would the idea benefit a large number of people or only a small group?
concepts.hint: If people disagree about what India should do, how would you decide what is fair?
concepts.probe: What questions does thinking about national development involve?
concepts.causeChain: Individuals seek different goals -> different and conflicting notions of national development -> national development means deciding what is fair and just and who benefits

keyPoints.text: It is very important to keep in mind that different persons could have different as well as conflicting notions of a country's development.
keyPoints.followUp: Will everyone in a country agree on what progress for the nation should mean?

requiredEvidence: different as well as conflicting notions

checks.criterion: States that different persons can have different and even conflicting notions of a country's development.

Would the idea benefit a large number of people or only a small group? National development means thinking about these questions.
keyPoints.followUp: What questions should we ask when different ideas of development clash?

topics.title: How to compare different countries or states?

concepts.label: Per Capita Income and the World Bank
concepts.cardText: For comparing countries, income is considered one of the most important attributes, since more income is understood to mean more of all things people need. Total income is not useful for comparison because countries have different populations, so we compare average income: the total income of the country divided by its total population, also called per capita income. The World Bank's World Development Reports use this to classify countries: in 2024, countries with per capita income of US$ 66,500 and above are high income, and those with about US$ 2,300 or less are low-income. India, at about US$ 11,000, is a low middle income country.
concepts.hint: Why divide a country's total income by its population before comparing?
concepts.probe: What is per capita income, and how does the World Bank use it to classify countries?
concepts.causeChain: Countries have different populations -> total income misleads -> compare average (per capita) income = total income / total population -> World Bank classifies countries by per capita income

causeLinks.criterion: Connects countries having different populations to the need to compare average (per capita) income rather than total income.

keyPoints.text: For comparing countries, their income is considered to be one of the most important attributes. Countries with higher income are more developed than others with less income, based on the understanding that more income means more of all things that human beings need.

checks.criterion: States that income is considered one of the most important attributes for comparing countries, because more income is taken to mean more of all things people need.

keyPoints.text: For comparison between countries, total income is not such an useful measure. Since countries have different populations, comparing total income will not tell us what an average person is likely to earn. Hence, we compare the average income which is the total income of the country divided by its total population. The average income is also called per capita income.
keyPoints.followUp: Why is total income not a good way to compare countries, and what do we use instead?

requiredEvidence: total income of the country divided by its total population

checks.criterion: Explains that total income is not useful for comparing countries because they have different populations.
Defines average or per capita income as the total income of the country divided by its total population.

Countries with per capita income of US$ 66,500 per annum and above in 2024 are called high income or rich countries and those with per capita income of about US$ 2,300 or less are called low-income countries. India comes in the category of low middle income countries because its per capita income in 2024 was just about US$ 11,000 per annum.
keyPoints.followUp: How does the World Bank use income to group countries, and where does India fall?

checks.criterion: States that the World Bank's World Development Reports classify countries by per capita income into high income (rich) and low-income countries.

concepts.label: Averages Hide Disparities
concepts.cardText: Averages are useful for comparison, but they also hide disparities. Countries A and B can have the same average income: in A, citizens are neither very rich nor extremely poor; in B, most citizens are poor and one person is extremely rich. Most of us would prefer to live in A because it has a more equitable distribution. So while average income is useful for comparison, it does not tell us how income is distributed among people.
concepts.hint: Two countries have the same average income. Would you be equally happy to live in both?
concepts.probe: Why can average income mislead us about how well off people in a country are?
concepts.causeChain: Average income can be the same for two countries -> but distribution differs (equitable in A, one rich and many poor in B) -> average does not show distribution -> averages hide disparities

causeLinks.criterion: Uses the example of two countries with the same average income but different distributions to explain why averages hide disparities.

keyPoints.text: Country A and country B have identical average income. Country A is preferred because it has more equitable distribution: people are neither very rich nor extremely poor. In country B, most citizens are poor and one person is extremely rich.
keyPoints.followUp: If two countries have the same average income, why might we still prefer one of them?

checks.criterion: Explains that two countries can have the same average income while one has an equitable distribution and the other has many poor people and one very rich person.

keyPoints.text: While 'averages' are useful for comparison, they also hide disparities. While average income is useful for comparison it does not tell us how this income is distributed among people.

requiredEvidence: does not tell us how this income is distributed

checks.criterion: States that averages are useful for comparison but hide disparities: average income does not show how income is distributed among people.

concepts.label: Income and Other Criteria: Kerala and Haryana
concepts.cardText: Haryana has the highest per capita income of Haryana, Kerala and Bihar, and Bihar the lowest. By income alone, Haryana would be the most developed. But in Kerala, 6 of every 1000 children die before age one, against 28 in Haryana, nearly three times more. About one-third of children aged 15-17 in Bihar are not attending school. So, besides average income, we must consider other attributes like health and education. The Infant Mortality Rate is the number of children who die before age one per 1000 live births.
concepts.hint: Haryana earns more per person than Kerala. Who does better on infant deaths?
concepts.probe: Why is per capita income alone not enough to compare the development of Haryana and Kerala?
concepts.causeChain: Haryana has higher per capita income than Kerala -> but Kerala has a much lower Infant Mortality Rate -> income alone does not show health and education -> other criteria are needed

causeLinks.criterion: Contrasts Haryana's higher per capita income with Kerala's much lower Infant Mortality Rate to show that income alone is not enough.

keyPoints.text: When we think of a nation or a region, we may, besides average income, think of other equally important attributes. Of Haryana, Kerala and Bihar, Haryana has the highest per capita income and Bihar is at the bottom; if per capita income were the measure, Haryana would be the most developed.

requiredEvidence: Haryana has the highest per capita

checks.criterion: Notes that Haryana has a higher per capita income than Kerala (and Bihar the lowest), so by income alone Haryana would seem most developed.

keyPoints.text: In Kerala, out of 1000 children born, 6 died before completing one year of age, but in Haryana the proportion was 28, nearly three times more. About one-third of the children aged 15-17 years in Bihar are not attending school in secondary classes.
keyPoints.followUp: How do Kerala and Haryana compare on children's health, and what does that show about using income alone?

checks.criterion: States that Kerala has a much lower Infant Mortality Rate than Haryana (6 against 28 per 1000 live births).
Mentions that about one-third of children aged 15-17 in Bihar are not attending school.

keyPoints.text: Infant Mortality Rate (or IMR) indicates the number of children that die before the age of one year as a proportion of 1000 live children born in that particular year. Literacy Rate measures the proportion of literate population in the 7-and-above age group. Net Attendance Ratio is the number of children of age group 15-17 years attending school as a percentage of all children in that age group.

checks.criterion: Defines the Infant Mortality Rate as the number of children who die before the age of one per 1000 live births.
Defines the Literacy Rate as the proportion of literate population aged 7 and above, or the Net Attendance Ratio.

concepts.label: Public Facilities
concepts.cardText: Money in your pocket cannot buy all the goods and services you need to live well. It cannot normally buy a pollution-free environment or ensure unadulterated medicines, or protect you from infectious diseases unless the whole community takes preventive steps. For many important things, the best and cheapest way is to provide them collectively, like security for a whole locality or schools for all children. Kerala has a low Infant Mortality Rate because it has adequate basic health and educational facilities; where the Public Distribution System functions well, health and nutrition are likely to be better.
concepts.hint: Can your own money buy you clean air or protection from an epidemic?
concepts.probe: Why is income not a completely adequate indicator of the goods and services citizens can use? Explain with public facilities.
concepts.causeChain: Money cannot buy many goods and services (clean environment, pure medicines, protection from disease) -> best and cheapest to provide them collectively -> states with good public facilities (Kerala, working PDS) do better on health

causeLinks.criterion: Connects collective provision of health and education facilities to Kerala's low Infant Mortality Rate.

keyPoints.text: Money in your pocket cannot buy all the goods and services that you may need to live well. So, income by itself is not a completely adequate indicator of material goods and services that citizens are able to use. Normally, your money cannot buy you a pollution-free environment or ensure that you get unadulterated medicines, or protect you from infectious diseases unless the whole of your community takes preventive steps.

checks.criterion: Explains that money cannot buy all goods and services needed to live well, for example a pollution-free environment, unadulterated medicines or protection from infectious diseases.

keyPoints.text: For many of the important things in life the best way, also the cheapest way, is to provide these goods and services collectively. It is cheaper to have collective security for the whole locality than for each house to have its own security staff. You are able to study because many people believe the government should open schools so that all children have a chance to study.

concepts.label: Human Development Report
concepts.cardText: Income is important but an inadequate measure of development, so health and education indicators are now widely used along with income. The Human Development Report published by UNDP compares countries based on the educational levels of the people, their health status and per capita income. Sri Lanka, a small neighbour, is much ahead of India in every respect, and Nepal and Bangladesh have lower per capita income than India but better life expectancy. By prefixing 'Human' to development, the report makes clear that what matters is what happens to the citizens of a country.
concepts.hint: What three things does UNDP look at? How is that different from the World Bank?
concepts.probe: How is the UNDP's measure of development different from the World Bank's? What does it show about India and its neighbours?
concepts.causeChain: Income is an inadequate measure of development -> UNDP's Human Development Report adds health and education to per capita income -> Sri Lanka ahead of India; Nepal and Bangladesh better in life expectancy -> focus on people's health and well-being

causeLinks.criterion: Connects income being an inadequate measure of development to the UNDP comparing countries on education and health along with per capita income.

keyPoints.text: Even though the level of income is important, yet it is an inadequate measure of the level of development. Over the past decade or so, health and education indicators have come to be widely used along with income as a measure of development.
keyPoints.followUp: Is income enough to measure how developed a country is? What else is now used?

checks.criterion: States that income is important but an inadequate measure of development, so health and education indicators are used along with income.

keyPoints.text: Human Development Report published by UNDP compares countries based on the educational levels of the people, their health status and per capita income. Life expectancy at birth denotes the average expected length of life of a person at the time of birth.

checks.criterion: States that the UNDP's Human Development Report compares countries on educational levels, health status and per capita income.

concepts.label: Sustainability of Development
concepts.cardText: We want development to go up, or at least be maintained for future generations, but scientists warn that the present type and levels of development are not sustainable. Groundwater is a renewable resource, replenished by rain, but it can be overused: nearly one-third of India is overusing its groundwater, especially in Punjab and Western U.P. Non-renewable resources, like crude oil, have a fixed stock and will be exhausted; world reserves would last only about 50 years more. Environmental degradation does not respect national or state boundaries.
concepts.hint: What happens if we use more groundwater than the rain replaces? Can crude oil be replaced?
concepts.probe: Why is the issue of sustainability important for development? Explain with groundwater and crude oil.
concepts.causeChain: Present development overuses resources -> groundwater used faster than rain replenishes it; crude oil is a fixed, non-renewable stock -> resources run out -> development cannot be maintained for future generations

causeLinks.criterion: Connects using resources faster than they are replenished (or exhausting a fixed stock) to development not being sustainable for future generations.

keyPoints.text: We would like the level of development to go up further or at least be maintained for future generations. However, since the second half of the twentieth century, a number of scientists have been warning that the present type, and levels, of development are not sustainable.
keyPoints.followUp: What warnings have been given about the way we are developing today?

checks.criterion: States that development should be maintained for future generations, but scientists warn the present type and levels of development are not sustainable.

keyPoints.text: Groundwater is an example of renewable resources, which are replenished by nature. However, even these resources may be overused: if we use more than what is being replenished by rain, we would be overusing it. Nearly one-third of the country is overusing their groundwater reserves, particularly in the agriculturally prosperous regions of Punjab and Western U.P.
keyPoints.followUp: How can a resource that nature renews, like groundwater, still run short?

checks.criterion: Explains that renewable resources like groundwater can be overused if we use more than is replenished by rain.
Mentions groundwater overuse in India, for example nearly one-third of the country or Punjab and Western U.P.

keyPoints.text: Non-renewable resources are those which will get exhausted after a few years of use. We have a fixed stock on earth which cannot be replenished. Crude oil is a non-renewable resource; the world's reserves would last only 50 years more at the present rate of extraction. Countries like India depend on importing oil, so if prices of oil increase this becomes a burden.
keyPoints.followUp: What happens to resources that nature cannot renew, like crude oil?

checks.criterion: Explains that non-renewable resources such as crude oil have a fixed stock and will get exhausted (world reserves would last only about 50 years more).

keyPoints.text: Consequences of environmental degradation do not respect national or state boundaries; this issue is no longer region or nation specific. Our future is linked together. Sustainability of development is comparatively a new area of knowledge.

checks.criterion: States that the consequences of environmental degradation do not respect national or state boundaries; our future is linked together.
